brief.topic: The Chessboard That Defeats Every Domino Arrangement

creative.audience: Curious teens and adults; concrete visual reasoning before specialist terminology.
creative.learning_goal: A color invariant rules out every possible tiling.

scenes.narration: Sixty two squares. Thirty one dominoes. The area is perfect. So why can this board never be covered? Start with an ordinary chessboard, then remove two opposite corners. Every domino must cover two neighboring squares. No overlaps, no gaps, and no cutting the pieces. You could spend all night rearranging them. But there is a way to reject every arrangement at once. Look at what a single domino is forced to do.

Forget the whole board for a moment. Put one domino down horizontally. It covers one dark square and one light square. Turn it vertically. Still one of each. Every legal placement has this property, because neighboring squares have opposite colors. So a pile of thirty one dominoes must cover exactly thirty one dark squares and thirty one light squares. The pieces cannot negotiate that balance, no matter how cleverly we arrange them.

Now return to the two missing corners. On this eight by eight board, opposite corners have the same color. We removed two dark squares. That leaves thirty dark squares, but thirty two light squares. Pair each remaining dark square with a light one, and two light squares have no partner. This is not a failure to find a clever arrangement. It is a proof that every arrangement fails. The area matches. The color balance does not.

Change the puzzle: remove two neighboring corners along the top edge instead. Now one dark and one light square disappear. Can we tile this board? Yes. The six squares left in the top row pair off, and every complete row below pairs off too. Equal color counts alone do not guarantee that every imaginable shape can be tiled. But unequal counts immediately prove that it cannot. Before searching harder, look for something every legal move must preserve.
